tagline.text: Spanish-era lighthouse ruins and sea views on a headland in southwestern Guimaras

location.label: Location
location.text: Guisi Point (Sitio Guisi), Barangay Dolores, Nueva Valencia, Guimaras

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,800 (per person, day trip round trip from Iloilo including admission and lunch)

children.text: Guisi Lighthouse is the ruin of a Spanish-era lighthouse on a hill at Guisi Point, the southwestern tip of Guimaras, and is described as the second oldest lighthouse in the Philippines. Crumbling walls, a rusty spiral staircase, a newer lighthouse next door and Guisi Beach just below make it a quiet historic stop.

Guisi Lighthouse stands on a headland called Guisi Point in Barangay Dolores, Nueva Valencia, on the southwestern side of Guimaras. The island, which you can see across the water from Iloilo City, is best known for its mangoes, but once you reach its southern end, this ruin from the Spanish period is the most striking sight. The lighthouse was a navigation marker that helped ships travelling between Manila, Iloilo and Cebu pass safely through the Iloilo and Guimaras straits. Today it no longer shines, but that is exactly why you can look at a landscape layered with time in peace. Counting the boat from Iloilo City and the overland ride, a round trip takes more than half a day, so start early in the morning.

Many travel sources call this the second oldest lighthouse in the Philippines. The date of construction differs by source. One travel blog says the Spanish government built it in 1894–1896, while other sources say only that it dates from the Spanish colonial period. The Wikipedia entry for Nueva Valencia likewise says that during the Spanish era a lighthouse was placed near here to guide ships through the Iloilo Strait, and links this to the origin of the place name. The exact year of construction is not confirmed, so it is safest to think of it simply as a lighthouse from the Spanish colonial era. The old name "Faro de Punta Luzaran" that some blogs use also varies by source.

On arrival, the first thing you notice is a fish-shaped welcome sign at the entrance. Walking up the hill you reach mossy stone walls, the foundations of collapsed buildings, and ruins where trees and plants have grown into the walls. The centerpiece is the old rusty iron lighthouse tower, with a spiral staircase inside. According to one visitor's account, a sign said not to climb the tower, but the caretaker and the guide-driver gave permission and said it was safe, so the visitor went up. From the top, the Guimaras Strait and Guisi Beach to the lower right come into view at a glance. Because the structure is old and its materials may not be sturdy, always follow the local guidance.

Right beside it stands a white new lighthouse that still lights the shipping route. A few steps away is another tower that no longer works, so you can see old and new side by side. The atmosphere of the ruins also makes it known as a spot for wedding and pre-wedding photo shoots. Visitors on weekdays are said to be so few that you may have the place to yourself, so it suits anyone who wants a calm day, unlike the busy beach resorts. A short walk down from the lighthouse leads to Guisi Beach, so you can combine history and sea in one visit.

blocks.title: Old lighthouse tower and spiral staircase

children.text: The rusty iron tower and the spiral staircase inside are the heart of the ruins. There is a sign asking visitors not to climb, so first check with the caretaker and your guide that you have permission and that it is safe. Because the structure is old, climbing hard is not recommended.

Stone ruins with trees and plants growing through the walls are scattered across the hill. Traces of the old settlement are visible even from a distance, and photos are best in the afternoon when the sun is lower.

blocks.title: View of the strait from the tower

children.text: With permission, standing on top of the tower gives you a view of the blue water of the Guimaras Strait and Guisi Beach to the lower right.

The white new lighthouse is still in use, so you can capture the ruins and a working lighthouse in the same frame. Seeing the non-working tower beside it as well gives you the whole story of how the navigation marker changed.

A short walk down from the lighthouse leads to Guisi Beach with its clear water. One guide says that using the beach itself is free and separate from the lighthouse admission. After swimming, take your trash with you.
The texture of the ruins and the sea backdrop mean wedding and pre-wedding shoots are said to happen often. Ordinary visitors should wait a moment so as not to get in the way of a shooting team.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: From Iloilo City to the lighthouse and beach

children.text: Take a pump boat from Ortiz Wharf in Iloilo City across to Jordan Wharf. It takes about 15 minutes.
At the tourism office at Jordan Wharf, check transport and fares and arrange a tricycle tour or a van.
Head toward Dolores and arrive at Sitio Guisi. Pay the admission fee at the entrance and walk around the ruins.
With the caretaker's guidance, see the area around the tower and the viewpoints, and photograph the new lighthouse.
Go down to Guisi Beach and relax by the sea.
Head to the Alubihod Beach area and have lunch.
Return to Jordan Wharf, check the time of the last boat to Iloilo, and cross.
Some visitors report that jeepneys run only from the morning to the early afternoon, so decide your return time in advance.
Arrive in Jordan, visit the Trappist Monastery first and buy souvenirs.
Head down to Nueva Valencia, have lunch and leave your bags at your lodging.
See the Guisi Lighthouse ruins and walk along Guisi Beach.
Watch the sunset and have dinner around Alubihod Beach.
Hire an island-hopping boat to tour the Taklong marine reserve area, then return to Iloilo.
Direct flights run from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Iloilo International Airport (ILO). Guimaras has no airport, and there are no direct flights from Manila to Guimaras.
Iloilo airport is in Cabatuan, away from the city center. According to one blog, the shuttle van from the airport to SM City Iloilo cost about
, so check the current fare locally.
From SM City, go to Ortiz Wharf by jeepney or taxi.

Some visitors also report that from Sitio Guisi it is a gentle uphill walk of about 15 minutes to the lighthouse.
The lighthouse is an outdoor ruin, so the weather matters a great deal. The blue of the strait and the white new lighthouse look sharpest on clear days, so the dry season is the best time to go.
Some visitors report that unpaved sections turn to mud in the rainy season. Road conditions can be poor, so avoid rainy days.

There is almost no lodging right next to Guisi Lighthouse, so most people come as a day trip from Iloilo City or stay at a resort around Alubihod Beach. Alubihod is the signature beach of Nueva Valencia, with beach resorts and bungalows clustered along it. One guide says beach cottages usually start from
, so check before booking. There is also small lodging in the town of Jordan.

Restaurants are few in the countryside. Small shops and resort restaurants near Guisi Beach are the usual options, so it helps to bring water and snacks. Guimaras is famous for mangoes, so a mango festival is held in April, and when the season is right, some places sell mango pizza or desserts. Mango jam sold at the Trappist Monastery in Jordan is a popular souvenir.
Some visitors report that jeepneys run only from the morning to the early afternoon, so fix your return transport in advance.
You pay the admission fee in cash to the caretaker. He may not have change, so prepare small bills.
Before climbing the tower, always confirm permission and safety with the caretaker and your guide.
Wear sneakers or non-slip sandals, and bring a hat and sunscreen because the sun is strong.
Rural roads are unevenly paved, and tricycles reportedly sometimes get flat tires. Leave some buffer in your schedule.
Asking the tourism office at Jordan Wharf about fares and routes first reduces the worry about being overcharged.
Withdraw cash in Iloilo City beforehand. It may be hard to withdraw cash locally.
The lighthouse itself takes about an hour, so combining Guisi Beach, Alubihod Beach and the Trappist Monastery into a one-day course makes the travel time worthwhile.
One blogger said the tricycle driver also acted as a guide on site, so ask the driver about the story of the ruins to get an explanation.
This is an old ruin and the structure may be weak. Follow the caretaker's instructions where a sign says not to climb, and avoid slippery stairs after rain.
The year of construction and the ranking (second oldest) differ by source, so refer to the local signboard or the caretaker's explanation.
The admission fee, contact number and opening hours come from sources around 2020 and may have changed. Check the latest information at the Jordan tourism office.
Boat service and fares vary with weather and season. In rainy weather there may be cancellations or delays.
There is little shade near the beach, so watch out for heatstroke and UV.
Take your trash with you and do not scribble on the stones or structures of the ruins.
The latter part of the road from Jordan Wharf to Guisi has unpaved sections with a lot of bouncing. If you get motion sick easily or have back problems, prepare in advance.
You can tour the whole island, with its mangoes, monastery and beaches, in one or two days. It is only about
15 minutes
by boat from Iloilo, so access is easy.
The central city of Western Visayas with the airport and wharf, and the starting point for a Guimaras trip.
The signature beach of Nueva Valencia, with resorts and bungalows that are good for lunch or an overnight stay.
An island reserve south of Nueva Valencia, and a boat tour route where you can see mangroves and coral.
